questions.q: What happens when both azurerm and aws are declared in the same required_providers block and used in the same configuration?
options: Terraform refuses to run because a config can only use one provider
Each provider automatically gets its own separate state file
Terraform builds one dependency graph across every resource in the file and plans/applies both clouds together from one state file
Only the first provider listed is actually used
questions.explain: Terraform doesn't care which API a provider talks to — it builds a single dependency graph covering every resource declared, regardless of provider, and plans/applies them together.

questions.q: Why does a design needing resources in both us-east-1 and us-west-2 require a provider alias, while using azurerm and aws together does not?
options: us-west-2 is not a valid Terraform region
A single provider "aws" {} block can only hold one region value, so a second region needs a second, aliased configuration of the same provider
azurerm and aws can't be used together without an alias
Provider aliases are required any time more than one resource exists
questions.explain: region can only be set once per provider block. Two regions of the same provider require two provider blocks — the second one declared with alias = to distinguish it from the default.

questions.q: What does provider = aws.east do on a resource block?
options: Creates a new provider alias on the fly
Has no effect unless required_version is also set
Restricts the entire configuration to the us-east-1 region
Routes that specific resource to the aliased aws provider configuration named "east" instead of the default one
questions.explain: provider = aws.east tells Terraform to use the aliased "east" aws provider block for that resource, rather than the default (unaliased) aws provider.

questions.q: What provider does a resource use if its block does not include a provider = argument?
options: A randomly selected aliased provider
No provider — the resource fails to plan
Whichever provider block appears last in the file
The default, unaliased provider block for that resource's type
questions.explain: A resource with no provider = argument automatically uses the default (unaliased) provider configuration for its resource type.

questions.q: What is the real use case this lesson gives for provider aliases, beyond the syntax itself?
options: A disaster-recovery design with a primary instance in one region and a standby in another, managed with the same credentials from one state file
Avoiding the need for required_providers altogether
Running two completely unrelated Terraform projects at the same time
Replacing the need for a resource group entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's real-world case is a primary/DR pair across two regions (us-east-1 and us-west-2) of the same AWS account, planned and applied together via aws.east and aws.west.
